News global nation business lifestyle entertainment technology sports opinion LATEST NEWS STORIES HEADLINES METRO REGIONS NATION WORLD CDN NEWSLETTER www / West Philippine Sea West Philippine Sea ‘Voldemort’ in WPS can now be named – Tarriela By: Gabryelle Dumalag - @inquirerdotnet INQUIRER.net / 05:35 AM November 18, 2026 Share: MANILA, Philippines — Less than a month after the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) urged Philippine officials to exercise restraint in their statements against China concerning the West Philippine Sea (WPS) dispute, one of the most vocal among them made a fresh, stinging pushback.
Speaking at a forum on Tuesday, Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said “aggressors” in the WPS can be likened to the character Voldemort, the villain in the popular “Harry Potter” novels and movies.
The analogy drew an immediate objection from a Chinese guest—and a Potter fan—sharing the stage with Tarriela.

The PCG official was speaking at the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea, a forum organized by the We Protect our Seas Foundation, Stratbase ADR Institute, the Department of National Defense and other think tanks.
“Right now, the international community no longer hesitates to call out who is Voldemort, who is aggressor, who is the victim, and who is the bully,” Tarriela said.
READ: West PH Sea: Oban urges 5-year plan to uphold South China Sea rules
He said the Philippine government’s “transparency campaign” had encouraged foreign governments to openly identify those responsible for aggressive actions at sea, unlike before when they avoided naming the countries involved.
He likened such reluctance to the fear of mentioning Voldemort or “He Who Must Not Be Named,” referring to a plot point in the Potter series.
“Voldemort is so powerful that they cannot even mention his name,” said Tarriela, who noted how governments then issued broad statements on South China Sea tensions without openly naming the aggressors.
“Those who violate the international law is Voldemort,” he said.
Responding to Tarriela, Sophie Wushuang Yi of the Beijing-based Grandview Institution said: “I’m really saddened to hear the comparison between Voldemort or you know who.”
Describing herself as a longtime Harry Potter fan who spent 11 years in the United Kingdom, Yi questioned the kind of labeling Tarriela used in geopolitical discourses.
“One country’s defense is another’s offense. One’s Voldemort is perhaps one’s Dumbledore,” she said.
She cited, for example, Beijing’s concern over the joint military exercises by the Philippines, the United States and Japan—as well as other “Balikatan” exercises which she said had grown in scale and has since involved other participating countries.
On Nov. 8, the DFA issued a statement reminding Philippine officials to “align” their public statements with the foreign policy direction of President Marcos.
The department reminded civilian and military officials of their responsibility to follow the administration’s diplomatic approach to the tensions complicating the country’s relations with China.
The statement followed a Nov. 3 telephone conversation between Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, on the heels of an escalating word war between Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan and Philippine defense officials as well as lawmakers.
But the DFA also acknowledged the transparency campaign conducted by the government’s defense agencies, which had served to document and expose incidents of aggression in the West Philippine Sea.
